prompt.context: Your client is a U.S. defense contractor that manufactures the Mohawk Light Fighter Jet for the British Royal Air Force. The company has produced the $20 million fighter jet for the past 12 years. The British government has decided to put the contract out to bid, however, and to win the program, the client's purchasing agents have estimated the company will need to cut its costs by 5 percent. It has asked BCG to help it reduce costs.
prompt.question: How should the client reduce its costs by 5 percent in order to win the re-bid contract for the Mohawk Light Fighter Jet?

clarifying_info.q: Is BCG's role also to verify the purchasing department's 5% estimate?
clarifying_info.a: No, you can assume that the purchasing estimate is correct. BCG's role is to find the cost savings to meet that estimate.

clarifying_info.q: Are there restrictions on who the client can purchase materials from?
clarifying_info.a: The British Ministry of Defense (MOD) allows 'commercial off-the-shelf' purchases, meaning the client is free to purchase from whomever it wants, as long as parts meet MOD quality guidelines.

clarifying_info.q: What is the difference between components and subassemblies?
clarifying_info.a: A subassembly functions on its own (e.g., the pilot night vision system). A component is a smaller part, such as a part of the engine.

clarifying_info.q: How many suppliers are there for the major subassemblies?
clarifying_info.a: There are seven suppliers of major subassemblies that go into the fighter jet.

clarifying_info.q: Could new suppliers enter to compete for the subassembly work?
clarifying_info.a: The manufacture of these parts requires a substantial investment in R&D, engineering, and infrastructure. It would be very costly for new suppliers to make the required investment.

clarifying_info.q: What share of subassembly manufacturers' costs are purchased materials?
clarifying_info.a: Purchased materials average approximately 70 percent of the price paid to most of the subassembly manufacturers.

clarifying_info.q: How many raw material and component suppliers are there across the supply chain?
clarifying_info.a: There are approximately 125 suppliers of raw materials and components among the subassembly manufacturers and the client itself.

clarifying_info.q: Are the raw materials and components commodity or customized products?
clarifying_info.a: About 80 percent of these products are commodities, such as sheet metal and wire harnesses. Even some electronics such as printed wire boards and circuitry are fairly generic.

clarifying_info.q: Is there commonality in raw materials and components across the subassembly manufacturers?
clarifying_info.a: Approximately 30 percent of the cost of raw materials is from similar materials used across the subassembly manufacturers. Engineers believe the percentage of overlap could be increased substantially, particularly for basic materials such as screws and sheet metal, but also in more customized areas.

clarifying_info.q: Do the subassembly manufacturers use the same suppliers for overlapping materials?
clarifying_info.a: Although there are some common suppliers, the analysis indicates that the subassembly manufacturers tend to use different suppliers even for similar materials.

exhibits.title: Fighter Jet Cost Structure
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of the total cost of the $20 million fighter jet into major cost categories and subcategories
exhibits.data: Major categories include: Purchased Materials (largest share, >50% of total cost; subdivided into Purchased Subassemblies ~40% of jet cost, Components, and Raw Materials — subassemblies alone >70% of the materials bucket); Manufacturing (includes Direct Labor as a large sub-item); Overhead (includes Program Management and Corporate Overhead)

framework: 1. Understand the cost structure of the jet to identify where costs are concentrated
2. Identify the major cost drivers within each category
3. Explore feasible levers to reduce costs in the highest-impact areas
4. Quantify potential savings and assess whether the 5% target is achievable
5. Develop an implementation approach for the recommended initiatives

questions.prompt: How would you interpret the cost breakdown exhibit, and where would you focus first?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies Purchased Materials as the dominant cost driver (>50% of total), with Purchased Subassemblies representing the largest single line item (~40% of jet cost). Candidate should prioritize materials over overhead or labor given the relative magnitudes, and note that within overhead, Program Management and Corporate Overhead are notable sub-items.

questions.prompt: Purchased subassemblies comprise more than 70% of the materials bucket (~40% of jet cost). There are only 7 subassembly suppliers and high entry barriers. Where do you look for savings within materials?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that with only 7 suppliers and high barriers to new entry, direct price pressure on subassembly manufacturers is limited. The next logical move is to look one level deeper — at the raw materials and components purchased by both the client and the subassembly suppliers — where there may be more fragmentation and consolidation opportunity.

questions.prompt: If purchased materials are ~70% of subassembly manufacturers' costs, and subassemblies are ~40% of the jet cost, what share of the jet's total cost is raw materials and components (across the full supply chain)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should chain the percentages: subassembly manufacturers' purchased materials = 40% × 70% = 28% of jet cost. Adding client's own raw materials and components (~15% of jet cost) gives roughly 43% of total jet cost tied up in raw materials and components. A 20% reduction in these costs would yield ~8.6% cost reduction on the jet — exceeding the 5% target.

math.setup: Subassemblies = 40% of jet cost; purchased materials = 70% of subassembly cost; client's own raw materials and components = ~15% of jet cost
steps: Subassembly manufacturers' purchased materials: 40% × 70% = 28% of jet cost
Add client's own raw materials/components: 28% + 15% = ~43% of jet cost
Required savings to hit 5% target: 5% ÷ 43% ≈ 11.6% reduction needed in this pool
Illustrative target: a 20% reduction × 43% = 8.6% reduction in total jet cost, exceeding the 5% goal
math.answer: ~43% of jet cost is in raw materials and components; a 20% reduction in this pool saves ~8.6% of total jet cost, more than enough to hit the 5% target

questions.prompt: There are ~125 raw material and component suppliers across the supply chain, ~80% supplying commodities. Only ~30% of raw material costs are currently from materials common across subassembly manufacturers, though engineers believe overlap can be increased. Subassembly makers tend to use different suppliers even for similar items. What is your recommended approach to capture savings?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify purchase consolidation (leveraging combined volume across 7 subassembly manufacturers + client to negotiate better prices with fewer suppliers) as the primary lever. Key enablers: (1) increase design commonality — form cross-company engineering teams to standardize specs on screws, sheet metal, and other basic materials; (2) consolidate supplier base — shift volume from ~125 fragmented suppliers to fewer preferred suppliers; (3) use a bidding/e-procurement system for true commodities to drive competitive pricing. Candidate should acknowledge that commodities have thin margins so a 15-20% cost reduction may be challenging, and a fallback lever (direct labor / outsourcing) should be prepared.

brainstorming.prompt: Where else could the client look for cost savings if the raw materials purchasing initiative is insufficient?

categories.name: Direct Labor / Manufacturing
ideas: Increase use of purchased subassemblies to reduce in-house manufacturing (outsourcing)
Assess whether direct labor productivity can be improved through lean/process improvements
Evaluate whether any manufacturing steps can be moved to lower-cost locations

categories.name: Overhead Reduction
ideas: Reduce program management overhead by streamlining reporting and governance
Consolidate corporate overhead by sharing services across programs
Review administrative headcount relative to volume

categories.name: Design & Engineering
ideas: Redesign components to reduce material content or substitute lower-cost materials
Standardize parts across programs to increase volume and reduce per-unit costs
Reduce complexity in customized parts to lower supplier production costs

categories.name: Supply Chain Structure
ideas: Form a virtual/shared purchasing department (potentially internet-enabled) spanning the client and all 7 subassembly manufacturers
Run competitive e-auctions for commodity materials
Negotiate longer-term volume commitments in exchange for lower unit prices

recommendation: The client should pursue a two-track cost reduction program targeting the ~43% of jet costs residing in raw materials and components across the supply chain

Track 1: Consolidate purchasing — form a virtual purchasing organization (potentially internet-enabled) spanning the client and its 7 subassembly manufacturers, consolidate ~125 suppliers to fewer preferred suppliers, and run competitive bidding for commodity items; targeting a 15-20% cost reduction in this pool to deliver >5% savings on the jet

Track 2: Increase design commonality — establish cross-company engineering teams to standardize specs on basic materials (screws, sheet metal, wire harnesses, printed wire boards) and explore expanding the overlap beyond the current ~30% of raw material costs; this both enables Track 1 consolidation and may reduce material content
risks: A 15-20% cost reduction target may be aggressive given thin margins on commodity raw materials
Subassembly manufacturers must be willing to share engineering drawings, specs, and supplier information — requires trust and aligned incentives
If the client loses the contract regardless, investments in redesign and system implementation may not be recoverable
Upfront costs for design standardization and implementation of the shared purchasing system must be evaluated before committing
next_steps: Conduct detailed interviews with purchasing and engineering personnel at all 7 subassembly manufacturers to map cost structures and supplier lists
Analyze bills of materials across manufacturers to quantify the achievable commonality beyond the current 30%
Design and pilot a shared e-procurement platform for commodity materials
Evaluate direct labor / outsourcing opportunity in parallel as a contingency lever
